extracted.intended_audience: owners/operators of stationary combustion turbines and fossil fuel-fired EGUs; state and federal regulators; industry compliance and legal counsel; environmental stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements for New Source Performance Standards (NSPS) under 40 CFR part 60 (subpart TTTTa/TTTT) applicable to new, modified, and reconstructed stationary combustion turbines and fossil fuel-fired steam generating units, including emissions standards, monitoring, recordkeeping, compliance dates, and extension procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate-load combustion turbine emission standard (final)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is finalizing a standard of 1,170 lb CO2/MWh-gross for intermediate load combustion turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Agency considered, but rejected, finalizing an emissions standard of 1,190 lb CO2/MWh-gross because that level "would not require the most efficient available versions of new intermediate load simple cycle turbines and does not represent the BSER." The 1,170 lb value reflects achievable performance demonstrated by multiple manufacturers and installations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase-2 standard for base-load combustion turbines: 90% CCS
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA proposed and is finalizing that 90 percent CCS (capture system operational anytime the turbine is operating) qualifies as the second component of the BSER for base load combustion turbines; EPA reduced the emissions rate by 89 percent to determine the CCS-based phase-2 standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CCS percent reduction is based on a CCS system capturing 90 percent of the emitting CO2 being operational anytime the combustion turbine is operating. The standard of performance for base load turbines is adjusted based on uncontrolled emission rates of fuels relative to natural gas (see separate oil-fired adjustment). EPA solicited comment on a 75–90% reduction range but determined 90% is adequately demonstrated and appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fuel-specific adjustment to phase-2 standards (distillate oil example)
rubrics_metrics.description: For 100 percent distillate oil-fired combustion turbines, the EPA sets the phase-2 emission rate at 120 lb CO2/MWh-gross (adjusted from the gas-fired baseline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phase-2 standard for base load turbines is adjusted based on the uncontrolled emission rates of the fuels relative to natural gas; EPA applied this approach to oil-fired turbines as an example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstructed combustion turbines may comply via retrofit upgrades
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners/operators of reconstructed combustion turbines can use manufacturer upgrade packages (e.g., GE Advanced Gas Path, Siemens Hot Start on the Fly, Solar Turbines Gas Compressor Restaging) or retrofit technologies (e.g., steam injection, HRSG addition) to comply with intermediate load emission standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and descriptions: Advanced Gas Path retrofits increase durability, air sealing, and efficiency; Hot Start on the Fly software reduces startup times; compressor restaging adjusts compressor characteristics for efficiency; steam injection estimated at ~$250/kW and can be up to 60% smaller than a similar HRSG. Conversions from simple cycle to combined cycle (HRSG additions) are documented at multiple plants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costing assumptions for CCS retrofit on reconstructed turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA approximated adding CCS to a reconstructed combustion turbine by increasing capital costs of capture equipment by 9% relative to new construction, and decreasing net efficiency by 0.3 percent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the same costing assumptions as newly constructed combined cycle turbines, compliance costs for reconstructed combined cycle turbines are ~10% higher than comparable new turbines. Example compliance costs (assuming continued operation of capture): $17/MWh and $51/ton for a 6,100 MMBtu/h H-Class turbine; $21/MWh and $63/ton for a 4,600 MMBtu/h F-Class turbine. If capture system is not operated while subcategorized as intermediate load, costs are lower (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstructed turbine exemption for technological and economic infeasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A reconstructed stationary combustion turbine is not required to meet the standards if doing so is deemed to be 'technologically and economically' infeasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires a case-by-case reconstruction determination considering economic and technological feasibility. The determination considers identified BSER and technologies EPA considered (including those rejected as BSER) and may find site-specific options are feasible. Equipment upgrades and best operating practices may in some cases achieve sufficient reductions to meet reconstructed standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: No NSPS standards for modifications of combustion turbines in this final rule
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA did not propose or solicit comment on standards of performance for modifications of combustion turbines and is not establishing any in this final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 2015 EPA delayed issuing modification standards for combustion turbines due to lack of information and expectation that few sources would undertake NSPS modifications. EPA is not aware of evidence indicating owners/operators intend to undertake actions that would qualify as NSPS modifications in the future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards apply at all times (Startup, Shutdown, and Malfunction - SSM)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is finalizing standards in this rule that apply at all times; subpart TTTTa overrides general provisions that would exempt standards during startup, shutdown, and malfunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA interpreted CAA section 111 as requiring continuous standards and not requiring consideration of malfunctions (sudden, infrequent, not reasonably preventable events) when setting standards. EPA's analysis used CEMS data that includes all periods of operation (startup, shutdown, malfunction) and is therefore not establishing alternate standards for those periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed approaches to determine CO2 emissions (testing/monitoring options)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA allows three approaches for determining CO2 emissions: (1) CO2 CEMS and stack gas flow monitor; (2) hourly heat input, fuel characteristics, and F factors (for oil- or gas-fired EGUs); or (3) Tier 3 calculations using fuel use and carbon content (GHGRP approach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First two approaches are used under Acid Rain program (40 CFR part 75); Tier 3 is used under GHGRP (40 CFR part 98, subpart C). ECMPS reporting expects hourly/daily CO2 values and contains numerous electronic checks. EPA permits the heat-input/F-factor approach as an alternative to continuous CO2 CEMS/flow for oil/gas EGUs to avoid impracticality/space constraints and incremental costs (~$52,000 annualized to install continuous CO2/flow where none exist).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality assurance / quality control for CO2 measurement systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Each CO2 CEMS and stack gas flow monitor must undergo regular QA/QC activities including periodic relative accuracy test audits (RATA) comparing the EGU's monitoring system to an independent monitoring system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A May 2022 EPA study found the average difference between the EGU's monitoring system and the independent system was ~2% for CO2 concentration and slightly greater than 2% for stack gas flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: CCS-specific monitoring and reporting via GHGRP
rubrics_metrics.description: Any affected unit employing CCS that captures enough CO2 to meet the standard and injects it underground must report under GHGRP subpart RR or subpart VV; if the EGU sends captured CO2 offsite, it must transfer CO2 to a facility that reports under those GHGRP subparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance with the standard is determined exclusively by tons of CO2 captured by the emitting EGU (not tons sequestered at the geologic site). EPA leverages GHGRP reporting to verify captured CO2 is sent to a geologic sequestration site. This rule does not regulate downstream recipients; requiring transfer to GHGRP-reporting entities is an enforcement element to avoid duplicative MRV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping and reporting via ECMPS and retention of existing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: EGU owners/operators must prepare reports in accordance with ECMPS (Acid Rain Program) and submit quarterly; EPA is retaining existing recordkeeping requirements (40 CFR part 60.5560) and subpart F of part 75 provisions in new subpart TTTTa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA expects minimal incremental reporting cost because affected EGUs already participate in ECMPS/Acid Rain. If an EGU is not already covered by ECMPS, estimated annual per-unit cost is ~$8,500. EPA is finalizing addition of keeping records of electric sales to demonstrate not exceeding the threshold that would trigger the output-based standard, and is updating test method references (ANSI/ASME/ASTM) and adding SI equivalents where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance dates for new/reconstructed sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners/operators of affected sources that commenced construction or reconstruction after May 23, 2023 must meet the requirements of 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTTa upon startup of the new/reconstructed affected facility or the effective date of the final rule, whichever is later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This compliance schedule is consistent with section 111 of the CAA and aligns with EPA's determinations of reasonable lead times to install BSER technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase-2 compliance date extension process and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is finalizing a provision allowing owners/operators of new or reconstructed base load stationary combustion EGUs to request a limited Phase 2 compliance extension of up to 1 year (to no later than Jan 1, 2033) if they demonstrate necessity due to circumstances entirely beyond their control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests must be received at least 180 days before the Jan 1, 2032 Phase 2 date. The owner/operator must document that it has taken all steps possible to install/start up necessary controls and still cannot comply due to circumstances beyond its control (e.g., permitting delays, delays in delivery/construction of parts, infrastructure development such as CO2 pipelines). Documentation may include vendor/engineering firm statements, permit delay records, or infrastructure construction/permitting evidence. The extension is intended only for unavoidable delays, not for additional time to assess compliance strategy. If granted and the unit still cannot install/start controls by Jan 1, 2033, the unit may operate in the intermediate load subcategory (12-month capacity factor between 20–40%) and must comply with applicable intermediate-load standards until controls become operational.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER determination for coal-fired steam generating units (2018 Proposal withdrawal)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is withdrawing its 2018 Proposal that would have made the BSER for newly constructed coal-fired EGUs the most efficient available steam cycle plus best operating practices; EPA now concludes CCS is adequately demonstrated for coal-fired steam generating units and thus is not finalizing the 2018 change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA explains the 2018 Proposal had found partial CCS too costly and lacking geographic scope; EPA now no longer believes there is a basis for imposing less effective controls (highly efficient generation + best practices) for new coal-fired sources. EPA is considering potential future revisions to account for CCS improvements and tax credits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and treatment of 'large modification' for steam generating units
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'large modification' is defined as a physical change or change in method of operation that results in an increase in hourly CO2 emissions of more than 10 percent compared to the source's highest hourly emissions in the previous 5 years. Such units are required to meet a unit-specific CO2 emission limit determined by that unit's best demonstrated historical performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2015 NSPS established standards for large modifications and did not include standards for 'small modifications' (change resulting in ≤10% increase). EPA historically observed few modifications and concluded it lacked sufficient information to establish standards for all types of modifications at this time, focusing on larger modifications involving substantial increases (e.g., refurbishing/replacement of steam turbines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial and technical amendments to improve clarity and flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is finalizing less-significant amendments that are editorial or add compliance flexibility: define acronyms on first use, add SI equivalents for heat-input based standards, correct incorrect regulatory part references, require records of electric sales to demonstrate applicability, update ANSI/ASME/ASTM test method versions, and add compliance flexibilities for EGUs serving a common generator or using a common stack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These amendments do not change substantive requirements of subpart TTTT but are incorporated into final subpart TTTTa to improve clarity and practical compliance.
